newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African budget seen boosting growth potential.
newsitem.headline: S.African budget seen boosting growth potential.

text.p: South Africa's sustainable growth rate would rise from three percent to four percent if the measures announced by Finance Minister Trevor Manuel in his 1997/98 budget were implemented, an economist said on Thursday.

"This is still too low to counteract the vicious circle of rising unemployment and crime, but is an impressive step in the right direction," Board of Executors Asset Management economist Rob Lee said in his latest Investment Outlook.
"If implemented fully, the budget and its accompanying exchange control reforms will make a very significant contribution to South Africa's attempt to match political success with economic success."
The main threat to this more positive outlook would be a failure to bring down consumption spending, both by government and individuals.
"The key variables are implementation of the budget spending plans and private sector wage restraint," Lee said.
Lee said the emphasis on fiscal restraint was welcome in the face of the unsustainable rapid growth in domestic spending over the last two years.
This rapid growth cast doubt on the ability of the government to meet its stringent spending targets, while at the same time making its achievement even more vital.
"The planned cut in real state spending for 1997/98 must be carried through," Lee said.

"The relatively low increase in public sector wages (seven percent) and the substantial cut in defence spending, gives it some credibility, but it will be a tall order. Some overrun is likely, but substantial slippage will be damaging."
It would also be important for private sector wage settlements not to accelerate to compensate for higher inflation.
This meant that real wage increases would have to be zero, which would help slow consumer spending and credit extension while contributing to industrial competitiveness.
Lee said short-term interest rates should not be cut until there were clear signs that the growth in spending was under control.
He welcomed the partial lifting of exchange controls but said that there were as yet no significant concessions for the 15 billion rand or so tied up in emigrants blocked rands.
"It is now probable that capital controls (as opposed to prudential or regulatory constraints) will be effectively abolished within a reasonable investment time horizon," Lee said.

While Manuel had partly tried to soften the blow of fiscal drag on lower and middle income taxpayers, further efforts to reduce the tax burden were necessary to achieve targeted growth of six percent by the end of the decade.
The government's reluctance to increase value added tax (VAT) was understandable, but Lee speculated that the next phase of deficit reduction could well include an increase in the basic VAT rate.
Lee said that as the reform process continued, sustainable capital inflows were likely to increase while domestic savings rose to reduce the dependence on foreign inflows to finance growth.

Lee, who last year warned that South Africa was heading towards a debt trap, said that this was much less likely now given the commitment to privatisation, the lifting of exchange controls, better debt disclosure and improved revenue collection.
